\chapter{Please and Sorry}
\label{ch:pa-please-and-sorry}
\hlchaptermodality{33}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask politely with miharbani karke and apologise with maaf karo, translate both word for word, say which noun in each came from Persian and which from Arabic, and write changa and thik-thak in Gurmukhi.}

The reader produces the apology, translates it as make pardoned, names Arabic as the source of its noun against the Persian source of the previous session's, runs both courtesies against the single verb they share, and writes thik-thak from its now-complete letter set.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[miharbānī karke]{\pa{ਮਿਹਰਬਾਨੀ} \pa{ਕਰਕੇ} — a god's name inside the word for \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:PA-C33-miharbani-karke}



\begin{quote}
Ask for water the way the drinks chapter taught, with \emph{kirpā karke} in front of it. That courtesy is Sanskritic. Punjabi has a second one, heard at least as often, and it comes down the other road.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਮਿਹਰਬਾਨੀ}} — \emph{miharbānī} — \textbf{kindness, a favour}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਮ}}, \textbf{\pa{ਿ}}, \textbf{\pa{ਹ}}, \textbf{\pa{ਰ}}, \textbf{\pa{ਬ}}, \textbf{\pa{ਾ}}, \textbf{\pa{ਨ}}, \textbf{\pa{ੀ}}: \textbf{\pa{ਮਿਹਰਬਾਨੀ}}. Then \textbf{\pa{ਕਰਕੇ}}. Every shape is already yours, so this phrase is writable on sight.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਮਿਹਰਬਾਨੀ}} is Persian \emph{mihrbānī}, and it comes apart in three.

\emph{-ī} is the quality-making ending, the one on \emph{khushī}, met when you were pleased to meet someone. \emph{-bān} means \textbf{keeper}, the piece that turns \emph{bāġ}, \textquotedblleft{}garden,\textquotedblright{} into \emph{bāġbān}, \textquotedblleft{}gardener.\textquotedblright{} And \emph{mihr} means \textbf{love, affection}.

\emph{Mihr} is the piece worth stopping on. It descends from Avestan \emph{Mithra}, an Indo-Iranian divinity who guaranteed covenants, whose name in the other branch of the family is Sanskrit \emph{mitra}, \textquotedblleft{}friend\textquotedblright{} — the figure Roman soldiers carried west as \textbf{Mithras}. Punjabi's commonest please carries, three layers down, the name of the god who made promises binding.

You have met \textbf{\pa{ਦੋਸਤ}}, a Persian word for friend. \emph{Mitra} is what Sanskrit called a friend, and both continue that same ancient name.

\textbf{\pa{ਕਰਕੇ}} is \textquotedblleft{}having done,\textquotedblright{} from \textbf{\pa{ਕਰਨਾ}}. So the phrase means \textbf{having done a kindness} — exactly what the courtesy in front of \emph{pāṇī} meant, with a Persian noun where that one had a Sanskrit one.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Writing: assemble \pa{ਚੰਗਾ}}
Both letters that \emph{changā} was waiting for have now been traced. Build it in four moves: \textbf{\pa{ਚ}}, the tippi \textbf{\pa{ੰ}} above it, \textbf{\pa{ਗ}}, and the upright \textbf{\pa{ਾ}}. Written out: \textbf{\pa{ਚੰਗਾ}}.

Copy it once with the model visible. Cover the model, write it again, and compare only whether the tippi sits above the first letter and not the second.

Then write \textbf{\pa{ਅੱਛਾ}} once beside it, and look at what the two words share: a first letter that hangs a mark above the line.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{miharbānī karke} — please
  \item \emph{Request:} water, then tea, using this courtesy instead of the other
  \item \emph{Split:} \textbf{\pa{ਮਿਹਰਬਾਨੀ}} into its three pieces (\emph{mihr}, \emph{-bān}, \emph{-ī})
  \item \emph{Connect:} \emph{mihr} to Sanskrit \emph{mitra}, \textquotedblleft{}friend,\textquotedblright{} and to \textbf{\pa{ਦੋਸਤ}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask for something politely, the Persian way. (\emph{Miharbānī karke}.) What are the three pieces of the noun? (\emph{Mihr}, \emph{-bān}, \emph{-ī}.) Which Sanskrit word is \emph{mihr}'s twin? (\emph{Mitra}.) Write \textbf{\pa{ਚੰਗਾ}} once from memory.

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A8\%AE\%E0\%A8\%BF\%E0\%A8\%B9\%E0\%A8\%B0\%E0\%A8\%AC\%E0\%A8\%BE\%E0\%A8\%A8\%E0\%A9\%80}{Wiktionary: miharbani}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D9\%85\%D9\%87\%D8\%B1}{Wiktionary: mihr}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ttha]{\pa{ਠ} — the tongue curled back}

\label{lesson:PA-W09-thattha}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\pa{ਤ}} once — the \emph{t} made with the tongue against the teeth. Then write \textbf{\pa{ਡ}}, whose sound is made with the tongue curled back against the roof. Say \emph{ṭhīk-ṭhāk} aloud and notice that its \emph{ṭh} belongs to the curled-back family, not the teeth family.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — one letter}
Trace \textbf{\pa{ਠ}} twice and say \emph{ṭha}: tongue curled back, then a puff of breath. Two small circles hanging from the top line, one above the other.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Cover the models. Write \textbf{\pa{ਤ}}, then \textbf{\pa{ਠ}}. Compare only where your tongue goes for each one.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
One letter. The word that needs it twice comes back in the next session.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[māf karo]{\pa{ਮਾਫ਼} \pa{ਕਰੋ} — an Arabic word with a Punjabi verb behind it}

\label{lesson:PA-C33-maaf-karo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{miharbānī karke}, then say \emph{shukrīā}. One is Sanskritic, one is Perso-Arabic, and both are ordinary Punjabi. Recall \textbf{\pa{ਮਦਦ}} from the helping verb, which came the same road.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਮਾਫ਼}} — \emph{māf} — \textbf{pardoned, excused}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਮ}}, \textbf{\pa{ਾ}}, then \textbf{\pa{ਫ}} carrying its dot underneath: \textbf{\pa{ਮਾਫ਼}}. Then \textbf{\pa{ਕਰੋ}}. That dot is the pair bindi you placed for \textbf{\pa{ਫ਼ੋਨ}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਮਾਫ਼}} is Arabic \emph{muʿāf}, \textquotedblleft{}pardoned, excused.\textquotedblright{} It is a passive participle: the shape Arabic gives a word to mean \emph{having had this done to it}. Its three-consonant root is ʿ-f-w, \textquotedblleft{}to pardon, to efface, to wipe away.\textquotedblright{}

It travelled the road this book keeps returning to: Arabic into Persian, Persian into Punjab, arriving with the dot that marks its foreign consonant. \textbf{\pa{ਮਦਦ}}, the noun in \textquotedblleft{}to help,\textquotedblright{} came the same way.

\textbf{\pa{ਕਰੋ}} is \textquotedblleft{}do\textquotedblright{} as a command, from the same \textbf{\pa{ਕਰਨਾ}} behind \emph{karke} and \emph{madad karnā}. The whole phrase reads \textbf{make pardoned}: not a feeling reported, but an act requested.

Set the two courtesies of this chapter beside each other and the pattern is plain. \emph{Miharbānī karke} asks for a kindness to be done. \emph{Māf karo} asks for a pardon to be done. Punjabi builds its politeness out of the same verb both times, and takes the noun from a different tradition each time — one from Sanskrit, one from Arabic.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Writing: assemble \pa{ਠੀਕ}-\pa{ਠਾਕ}}
The curled-back letter has been traced, so the middling answer can be written. First half: \textbf{\pa{ਠ}}, the long \emph{ī} sign \textbf{\pa{ੀ}}, \textbf{\pa{ਕ}} — that is \textbf{\pa{ਠੀਕ}}. Second half: \textbf{\pa{ਠ}}, the upright \textbf{\pa{ਾ}}, \textbf{\pa{ਕ}} — \textbf{\pa{ਠਾਕ}}. Joined with a hyphen: \textbf{\pa{ਠੀਕ}-\pa{ਠਾਕ}}.

Copy it once with the model visible. Then cover it, write it again, and compare only the two vowel signs, since everything else repeats. The repetition is the point: an echo half is written out in full even though it carries no meaning.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{māf karo} — sorry, excuse me
  \item \emph{Translate:} the phrase word for word (make pardoned)
  \item \emph{State:} which half of the phrase is borrowed and which is inherited
  \item \emph{Run through:} both courtesies — \textbf{miharbānī karke}, \textbf{māf karo} — and name the source of each noun
  \item \emph{Recall:} the divinity hiding inside \emph{mihr} (\emph{Mithra}, Sanskrit \emph{mitra})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the Punjabi for sorry. (\emph{Māf karo}.) What does it mean word for word? (Make pardoned.) Which verb do both of this chapter's courtesies share? (\textbf{\pa{ਕਰਨਾ}}.) Write \textbf{\pa{ਠੀਕ}-\pa{ਠਾਕ}} once from memory.

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A8\%AE\%E0\%A8\%BE\%E0\%A8\%AB\%E0\%A8\%BC}{Wiktionary: maaf}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D9\%85\%D8\%B9\%D8\%A7\%D9\%81}{Wiktionary: muaf (Arabic)}.
\end{tcolorbox}
